scores.evidence: Asynchronous engine-native replication on-premises → cloud during coexistence. Switch to synchronous commit just before the planned failover
scores.rationale: Replication, failover, synchronous-commit-before-cutover, single-writer semantics and duplicate-message risks are all stated accurately, with technology-specific limits marked as assumptions and validated (V3/V4).

scores.evidence: What exactly does "without downtime" means? I assumed a write pause of ≤ 60 s is acceptable
scores.rationale: Directly solves the zero-downtime migration, resolves the key ambiguity sensibly with a clinical confirmation step, and the staged rehost is clearly buildable with explicit, justified deferrals.

scores.evidence: Exactly one writable primary database at all times. On-premises is the system of record until the Phase 3 cutover, the cloud after it. Never both
scores.rationale: Single-write-authority, DNS-based cutover, pinned single-instance jobs and phase dependencies are honored consistently across every section, including the documented E1 exception.

scores.evidence: Two full rehearsals on a production-sized copy... 0 lost or duplicated transactions against the load generator's ledger
scores.rationale: V0–V7 tie checkable thresholds to the specific risks (lag, lost bookings, failback, circuit loss), run before commitment, and reconciliation and cost checks continue after cutover.

scores.evidence: ASSUMPTION: a planned database failover usually takes seconds to tens of seconds. The CMIO or clinical operations must confirm
scores.rationale: Every figure is labeled ASSUMPTION/UNKNOWN/BASELINE, missing inputs are ranked by plan impact, and each key decision has a stated revisit trigger if the assumption fails.

scores.evidence: two databases accept writes at once ("split brain")... a missed or delayed patient visit that nobody notices
scores.rationale: Covers the domain's hardest failures — double-booking, duplicate SIU messages/reminders, replication divergence, circuit loss, PHI exposure — each with concrete detection (reconciliation, duplicate detector) and rehearsed recovery.

scores.evidence: Synthetic book/cancel checks run on both paths. Alerts go to the existing on-call
scores.rationale: Deployment, rollback, domain health signals and ownership are concrete and sized to one on-call rota, but clinical staff communication, training and on-site hypercare at go-live are missing.

scores.evidence: Tagged cost reports over 30 days of full production (compute, storage, egress, circuits, licences)
scores.rationale: Run-cost drivers, controls (tagging, rightsizing, reserved-capacity gating, ≤6-month double-run cap) are concrete and honestly labeled UNKNOWN, but engineering/build effort cost is not accounted for.

scores.evidence: Rollback: none after reverse replication stops; V6 guards this step. Point of no return is Phase 5, not this phase
scores.rationale: Decisions carry explicit reversibility ratings, irreversible ones (write authority, residency, decommission) get the most validation, and failback stays available until a guarded point of no return.

scores.evidence: Re-architecture (containers, services, a managed database the app isn't built for). Pulled forward when Phase 5 is done
scores.rationale: Pure rehost with feature freeze, re-architecture and autoscaling deferred with pull-forward triggers; every component (dual circuits, replication, waves) is justified by a stated clinical or availability need.

scores.evidence: Route user groups by AD group, smallest first: IT and scheduling super-users → one low-volume outpatient clinic → 10% of call-centre seats
scores.rationale: Dependency-ordered phases with concrete first steps, checkable exit criteria at every stage, and explicit fallback paths (e.g., V1 fails → app and database move together) a team could execute immediately.

checklist.evidence: BAA covers every service in use... keys managed by the hospital... least-privilege database login... audit logs reaching the SIEM verified
a dependency inventory lists every interface, batch job, report extract, printer or label server, call-centre phone integration, reminder vendor, portal, warehouse extract
daily reconciliation of per-table row counts and checksums, plus appointment counts per resource per day... lag p99 < 5 s at peak
Exactly one writable primary database at all times... Never both. A short write pause is preferred over two databases accepting writes
Reverse replication cloud → on-premises starts at the cutover... Two full rehearsals... including failback; then the production go/no-go checklist
Two physically diverse private circuits plus a VPN backup... p95 ≤ 1.2× the on-premises BASELINE, per top-10 transaction
Cloud DR test: zone failover plus a point-in-time restore against the BC/DR RTO/RPO... downtime reports keep printing locally from the cloud
Identity federated with AD and least-privilege roles... Elevated access during the cutover only, with time limits
load test at 2× BASELINE peak over the real circuit... Each wave lasts at least one week including a Monday peak
a CAB slot outside known peaks (flu season, month-end)... Freeze schema and config changes... Planned failover in a low-volume window
Vendor support statement for running in the cloud... Wipe storage media to NIST 800-88 with certificates

traps.evidence: Move the tiers separately. First the cloud app tier serves groups of users against the on-premises database
Never both. A short write pause is preferred over two databases accepting writes
No clinical users, and no patient data at rest in the cloud... V2 must pass before the replica is seeded
Smoke-test every inventoried interface; run reconciliation within 1 h
Keep the existing architecture... Re-architecture... Pulled forward when Phase 5 is done

note: An exemplary, correctness-first staged rehost that avoids all traps; the only notable gaps are break-glass/MFA detail, clinical staff communication and hypercare, and build-effort cost accounting.
